title: Identifying Subject and Predicate - 4
text:
Sentences › Identifying Subject and Predicate › Identifying Subject and Predicate — Revision note (part 1/1)

Any sentence is constructed by joining small parts. The basic parts of any sentence is a subject, a verb, and an object. When these three come together, they form a complete sentence.

A **sentence** can be broadly divided into two parts. The **subject** and the **predicate**.

The **subject** is the person or thing, that is doing an action, or or the person or thing that is the focus of the sentence.

A **predicate** is the part of the sentence that contains the action. The predicate is formed by joining the verb and the object.

For example

The boy is hiding behind the table.

Here the subject is **'the boy'**and **'is hiding behind the table'**is the predicate which contains the verb _is hiding_and the object _table_.

Examples:

| **SUBJECT** | **PREDICATE** |
| --- | --- |
| The laptop | is kept for charging. |
| Milk | is good for health. |
| Agra | is known for the Taj Mahal. |
| Meera | is feeling tired and wants to sleep |

title: Collective Noun
text:
Nouns › Collective nouns › Collective nouns — Revision note (part 1/1)

A collective noun is used to refer to an entire group of persons, animals or things; it therefore includes more than one member.

For example, a ‘family’ has parents and children.

A ‘pack’ contains many wolves.

Example-

- People: crowd, team, choir, class, committee, family, group
- Animals: flock, herd, swarm, litter
- Things: bunch, collection, pack, set.

**More examples of collective nouns:**

A team of players.

A herd of cows

A flock of sheep

A fleet of ships

**Use of verb with Collective Nouns:**

_A plural collective noun takes a plural verb:_

Example- Families (Plural) come(Plural verb) tothis restaurant.

_A singular collective noun usually takes a singular verb:_

Example- Our family (singular) often comes (singular verb) to this restaurant.

title: Gender - 4
text:
Nouns › Gender › Gender — Revision note (part 1/1)

**There are four types of Genders:**

1. Masculine Gender
2. Feminine Gender
3. Neuter Gender
4. Common Gender

**Masculine Gender:**The Masculine Gender denotes the names of all male persons or animals. Example: man, actor, uncle, hero, king, lion etc.

**Feminine Gender:**The Feminine Gender denotes the names of all female persons or animals. Example: woman, aunt, daughter, actress, queen, lioness etc.

**Neuter Gender:** Non-living things or things without life cannot be distinguished either as male or female; hence they are called the Neuter Gender. Example: house, knife, tree, chair, table, book, ball etc.

**Common Gender:**Names that can be used for both males and females are called the Common Gender. Example: child, parent, student, friend etc.

**Changing Masculine Noun to Feminine Noun:**

**1. By adding ‘ess’ to the Masculine**

Example: Lion- Lioness, Prince- Princess, Host- Hostess

**2. Sometimes the form is slightly changed before 'ess' is added**

Example: Master- Mistress, Actor- Actress, Tiger- Tigress, God- Goddess

**3. By a different word**

Example: King- Queen, Boy- Girl, Father- Mother, Sir- Madam

For example –

I live in **Chennai.**

**A Common Noun refers to people, places or things in general.**

For example –

For example –

**Laughter** is the best medicine.

title: Subject and Object Pronouns
text:
Pronouns › Subject and Object Pronouns › Subject and Object Pronouns — Revision note (part 1/1)

To avoid repeating the nouns we use pronouns. In other words, pronouns take place of nouns.

They are divided into two parts:

- Subject Pronoun
- Object Pronoun

**Subject Pronouns replace the subject in the sentence.**

**For instance: Mohit**loves to play cricket.

**‘He’**loves to play cricket.

In the first sentence,**‘Mohit’** is the subject and in the second sentence the subject is replaced by a pronoun **‘he’**. The pronoun used to replace the subject in the sentence is known as ‘Subject Pronoun’.

**Object Pronouns replace the object in the sentence.**

**For instance:**Pratik helps **Rohan to complete the project.**

Pratik helps**‘him’**to complete the project.

In the first sentence,**‘Rohan’** is the object and in the second sentence the object is replaced by a pronoun **‘him’**. The pronoun used to replace the object in the sentence is known as ‘Object Pronoun’.

**The following table contains examples of Subject and Object Pronouns:**

**Subject Pronouns**Iyouwetheyhesheit**Object Pronouns**meyouusthemhimherit

**Some Example sentences:**

- **I** am going to the market with **her**.

title: Identifying Verbs - 4
text:
Verbs › Identifying Verbs › Identifying Verbs — Revision note (part 1/1)

Verbs are words that show actions that are physical actions like _run_, _jump_, _work_and internal actions like _love, think, consider etc._ Without verbs, you cannot '_do'_ anything, '_feel'_ anything or even '_be'_ anything.

They are the center of all sentences and clauses and show what the subject is doing or feeling, even if they’re just _existing (being)_.

There are two categories of verbs:

**Dynamic (action) verbs -**These describe a physical action or activity.

e.g. eat, walk, play, jump etc.

I am **eating**a pie.

I **walk**a few kilometers everyday.

I **play** football on the playground.

I **jumped**into the pool.

**Stative (state-of-being) verbs -**Stative verbs describe a subject’s state or feeling.

e.g. want, need, like, understand etc.

I **want**to eat a cake.

I **need**to go to the doctor.

I **like**walking in the park.

I **understood**what my teacher was saying.

title: Main and Helping Verbs
text:
Verbs › Main and Helping Verbs › Main and Helping Verbs — Revision note (part 1/1)

Verbs may be divided into **Main Verbs and Helping Verbs.**

**Main Verbs** are the verbs which say something about a subject. They are action words and do not require other words to complete their action.

The cat **jumps** on the sofa.

Sita **runs** fast.

Mohit and Mohan**play** football in the ground.

**Helping Verbs are words used to help the main verbs in a sentence.**

They help the main verbs express a state or an action. They are also called **Auxiliary Verbs.**

**To be, do** and **have**verbs are the most common helping verbs.

**Use of to be verbs (is, am, are, was, were) –**

- **Is/am/are**are used in Present Tense and **was/were** are used in the Past Tense.
- To talk about names, age, feeling, nationality, professions and many more.

I **am** Rina. She **is** 15 years of age. He **was** a doctor by profession.

- To talk about state of being

She **is tall.** We **are** human beings.

**Use of do, does, did –**

- **Do/does** are used in the **Present Tense** and **did** is used in the **past tense**.
- These helping verbs are used to **ask questions**.

Do you study every day?

- They are used to indicate **negative sentences**.

She does not want to eat vegetables.

- They are used to **add emphasis** to the sentences.

I do finish my work in class.

**Use of have, has, had –**

- **Have/has** are used in the **Present tense** and **had**is used in the **Past tense**.
- These helping verbs are used to **show possession**.

She has long hair.

- They are used when we talk of**eating and drinking**

We have coffee every day.

- They are used with **Perfect tenses**

He has done his work.

title: Identifying Adjectives - 4
text:
Adjectives and Adverbs › Identifying Adjectives › Identifying Adjectives — Revision note (part 1/2)

Adjectives are describing words. They describe, quantify, identify or further define the qualities of nouns or pronouns.

Adjectives are mainly of five types:

1. Adjectives of Quality
2. Adjectives of Quantity
3. Demonstrative Adjectives
4. Possessive Adjectives
5. Interrogative Adjectives

1. Adjective of Quality

Adjectives of quality describe the characteristics of a noun. They tell us about a noun’s size, color, shape, taste, and more. Some examples are big, yellow, square, jealous, and sweet. They answer the question ‘What kind of?’

For example: “The **pink,round**box is mine.” Here, pink and round are descriptive adjectives that describe the box.

2. Adjective of Quantity

Adjectives of quantity describe the exact or approximate amount of a noun. Some examples include all, no, few, many, and little. THey answer the question 'How much?' Numeral adjectives give exact number amounts (e.g. three, five, seventh, twelfth). They answer the question ‘How Many?’.

For example: “There are **thirty** girls in our class.” Here, ‘thirty’ is a numeral adjective that describes the number of girls.

There is **some**milk in the glass. Here, ‘some’ is an adjective of quantity that describes the approximate quantity of milk.

3. Demonstrative Adjective

Demonstrative adjectives answer the question ‘which one?’ They point out particular nouns. Demonstrative adjectives are this, that, these, and those.

This is used when the noun is near and singular. That is used when the noun is far and singular. These is used when the noun is near and plural. Those is used when the noun is far and plural.

For example: “She wore **that** dress.” Here, that is a demonstrative adjective that points to a particular dress.

4. Possessive Adjective

title: Identifying Adjectives - 4
text:
Adjectives and Adverbs › Identifying Adjectives › Identifying Adjectives — Revision note (part 2/2)

Possessive adjectives are a type of pronoun. They explain ownership. Possessive adjectives include my, your, his, her, its, our, and their. There is a corresponding possessive adjective for each of the personal pronouns. They answer the question 'whose?'

For example: “I lost **my** book.” In this sentence, my is a demonstrative adjective that explains whose book was lost.

5. Interrogative Adjective

Interrogative adjectives appear in interrogative sentences i.e., questions. ‘What, which, and whose’ are interrogative adjectives. In direct questions, the adjective will appear at the beginning of the sentence next to the noun it modifies.

For example: “**Which** book will you buy?” In this case, which is an interrogative adjective that modifies the noun book.

An **adverb** is a word that modifies (describes) a verb, an adjective, another adverb or a whole sentence.

_happily, wildly noisily..._

_**Adverbs of Frequency**_- They answer the qusetion HOW OFTEN?

_**Adverbs of Place**_- They answer the qusetion WHERE?

_**Adverbs of Time**_- They answer the qusetion WHEN?

title: Conjunctions and Interjections - 4
text:
Conjunctions › Conjunctions and Interjections › Conjunctions and Interjections — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Conjunctions** are words that join two or more words, phrases or clauses.

Conjunctions are often used to join sentences together. The most common conjunctions include; and, or, but.

They join sentences and ideas together so that the writing and reading flows smoothly.

The seven _**coordinating conjunctions**_are “And, but, for, nor, or, so, and yet” (Remember FANBOYS)

Eg: The teacher dictated the notes _**and**_ we wrote it down.

A _**subordinating conjunction**_ always introduces a dependent clause. A dependent clause is a group of words that cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. Eg: although, because, when, before, which, since etc…

Eg: They gave him another book _**because**_ he had already read that one.

_**Correlative conjunctions**_ are grouped conjunctions. They come in pairs. Eg: either…or, if…then, whether…or, not only…but also etc…

Eg: You can _**either**_go for a cruise _**or**_ take a road trip.

- **Interjections** are words used to express strong feeling or sudden emotion.

They are included in a sentence usually at the start to express emotions like surprise, disgust, joy, excitement, or enthusiasm.

An interjection is not grammatically related to any other part of the sentence.

Eg:

_**Eureka**_! I got the sum.

_**Yeah**_, a beautiful present.

_**Woo-hoo**_, what a goal!

title: Punctuation, Capitalisation and Formatting - 4
text:
Punctuation, Capitalisation and Formatting › Punctuation, Capitalisation and Formatting › Punctuation, Capitalisation and Formatting — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Punctuations** include **full stops, capital letters, commas, semi-colon, question marks, exclamatory marks, apostrophe,**and many more.

It helps the readers to understand the meaning of the text clearly. It makes our written text logical and readable.

Not using proper punctuation marks can change the meaning of the entire text.

For example –

**tina’s three favorite things are eating her family and shopping.** (This means Tina loves to eat her family and shop)

**Tina’s three favorite things are eating, her family and shopping.** (This means Tina loves to eat and shop and she loves her family)

**Capitalisation** means to make the **first letter of the word** capital. It is used to show the readers the **importance of specific words.**

For example –

My mother will buy dresses for me in **Diwali.**

On **Fridays,** I visit my aunt’s house**.**

**Formatting**means the presentation of our **paragraphs, essays or letters**.

We write headings, paragraphs, quotations, and many more in our writing skills.

The way of our writing, the alignment that we show in our letters and the fonts that we use play a very important role in creating impactful writing.

**A letter looks like a letter and a paragraph looks like a paragraph only because it follows proper formatting.**

**Opening of the story**: It is impressive to begin your story by describing the setting/ character or using sounds or a proverb.

Eg: The park was empty, so silent as if all the birds and insects had deserted it. No children playing on the slides and swings. The creepers and wines wilting away. I felt suffocated under the monstrous banyan tree. (Describing setting)

Eg: Crunching and munching the potato chips leisurely lays there ‘the king of our house’. He’s such a couch potato that he wouldn’t leave the recliner even if the house is on fire. I don’t why God made brothers! To be precise, “lazy yet genius younger brothers”. (Describing character and sounds)

**Setting**: The place where story takes place. It could be a city, a village, a forest etc., or an imaginary like on other planet.

**Characters**: The characters are the people or animals in the story. It is better to keep less characters (2-3) and describe them well.

**Conflict**: The main character of the story faces a problem which is called a conflict. Eg: stuck in a flood, forgetting a wallet while in a new town, alone on an island, or animals trying to save themselves in a forest fire etc.,

**Climax**: It is when the problems reach to the peak and the character has to take some steps to solve them.

**Resolution**: It when the character is able to solve his problems.

**Ending**: It is the end of the story where all ends well. You may also have an ending that doesn’t end well. Such stories have a moral and teach the reader what one shouldn’t do. Make your ending attractive.

Eg: Finally, the day ended and we all returned home safely vowing never to go on a trip in life without our parents. (Happy ending with a moral)

title: Message Writing - 4
text:
Composition - V › Message writing › Message writing — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Message:**

- A short piece of information or communication written to someone or for somebody when you can't speak to him or her yourself.
- It contains important information in precise and lucid manner.

**_Format:_**

**Heading-----Date-----Time-----Salutations-----Body-----Sender**

1. Heading:- Write the word '**_Message_**' in BOLD and CAPITAL letters in the **_middle_** of the line.

2. Date:- To be mentioned on the**_left hand side_** of the Page.

3. Time:- Can be mentioned either on the **_Left hand side or Right hand side_** of the Page.

4. Salutation:- Before the BODY of the message, salutation **_addresses the reader_** like Dear Mom, Dear Dad etc

5. Body:- All the information that needs to be conveyed to the reader/the person you are unable to contact is mentioned.

Body of the message is **_Short and Crisp_**.Avoid using long sentences.

6. Sender:- Mention your name on the left-hand side of the Page.

**_Sample Message:_**

1. A telephonic conversation and a message for Raj in less than 50 words:

Meena: Can I speak to Raj? I am Meena from his school.

Ramya: I am sorry. He is not at home.

Meena: When will he be back?

Ramya: He will be here in an hour.

Meena: Could you please convey a message to him?

Ramya: Yes, I will.

Meena: He has to report at Circle stadium at 7.00a.m tomorrow. The tennis match starts at 8.00a.m. Please tell him to carry his ID card, a bottle of water and a change of clothes

Ramya: Yes I will convey the message to him.

Meena: Thank you

**Letter Writing**

We write letters to our friends, uncles, aunts and sometimes to teachers and Principals. Letter to the principal will differ in tone and style as compared to the letter written to a friend.

That is why we have two types of letter –the friendly or informal letter and the polite or formal letter.

**Sample Letter:**

Rita writes two letters—one to her classmate and another to her Principal.

$\begin{matrix} ToAFriend-InformalStyle \\ 27thJuly,2019\ HiMeena,\ Heartycongratulations!Youhave\ scoredbrilliantmarksintheannual\ examination.YouleftforNagpursoon\ aftertheexams.IamsohappythatI\ havesuchgoodnewstogiveyou.The\ classteacherreadoutyourmarksin\ theassemblyandweallclappedfor\ you!\ IwillsendyoutheProgresscardby\ post.Canyoubelieve,wearegoingto\ betogetherinStd.sixtoo!\ Givemyregardstouncleandaunty.\ \ Withlotsoflove,\ Rita\ \\ \end{matrix}$ $\begin{matrix} TothePrincipal-FormalStyle \\ ThePrincipal\ NewEraPublicSchool\ SamtaNagar,\ GoregaonEast,\ Mumbai-400063\ \ 27thJuly,2019\ \ DearMadam,\ Myfatherisinthearmy.Hehasbeen\ postedtoJaipur.Allofusareshifting\ toJaipurbytheendofthismonth.\ IrequestyoutoissueaSchoolLeaving\ Certificatetome,sothatIcanget\ admissiontoaschoolinJaipur.\ Thankingyou,\ \ Yoursobediently,\ RitaSharma\ ClassVIID\ RollNo:17 \end{matrix}$

**Every letter has four parts:**
 The salutation or how you begin the letter
 The date of the letter
 The body of the letter
 The subscription or the way you end the letter.

In her letter to her friend, Rita uses a friendly tone. Her salutation is warm and friendly. She uses exclamation marks to show her excitement in giving good news to her classmate. She closes the letter with her first name.
